heuristics.rule: Choose sunrise industries over sunset industries, regardless of specific company
heuristics.condition: When comparing offers across industries with different growth trajectories...
heuristics.action: Prioritize the offer in the growing industry, even if the specific company or salary is slightly inferior
heuristics.because: Industry trajectory determines your optionality — in a declining industry you lose the ability to switch employers on your own terms; in a growing industry you can always find the next job

heuristics.rule: Prioritize industry brand and company prestige over short-term salary when the salary gap is within an acceptable range
heuristics.condition: When two offers differ in company prestige but salary is within acceptable tolerance...
heuristics.action: Choose the higher-prestige company for the resume credential it provides
heuristics.because: Recruiters assess candidates by educational background AND company pedigree; a top-company background unlocks higher salary floors at the next job

heuristics.rule: Never factor in promised annual raises or unvested options when comparing offers
heuristics.condition: When an offer includes unvested equity or promises of future salary adjustments...
heuristics.action: Exclude those figures entirely from your comparison calculation; only count guaranteed, immediately vested cash
heuristics.because: Unvested options and future raise promises are 'big cakes' (画饼) — they are not guaranteed and should not affect a present-value comparison

heuristics.rule: Apply weighted scoring rather than raw scoring when comparing offers
heuristics.condition: When comparing multiple offers across several dimensions (salary, commute, team, growth, etc.)...
heuristics.action: Assign a personal importance weight to each factor, multiply each factor's score by its weight, then sum — do not just add raw scores
heuristics.because: Two offers with nearly identical raw totals can have drastically different weighted outcomes; raw totals obscure what actually matters to you

heuristics.rule: Clarify your core need before evaluating any offer dimension
heuristics.action: Explicitly articulate whether your primary goal is money, career capital, family stability, or passion — and build all evaluation criteria around that one goal
heuristics.because: Without anchoring on a core need, people unconsciously apply inconsistent weights and make decisions they later regret

heuristics.rule: Watch for stagnation signals at large companies before treating prestige as a universal positive
heuristics.condition: When a large-company offer seems prestigious but you notice employees staying at the same level for 3-4 years...
heuristics.action: Treat that as a red flag and reconsider whether the prestige benefit outweighs low internal mobility
heuristics.because: Some large companies offer brand value but trap employees in low-growth roles with minimal salary progression, negating the prestige advantage

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether you have future job optionality; a declining industry removes your ability to switch employers on favorable terms
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research industry hiring trends, VC funding flows, headcount growth at top companies in the sector over the past 3 years

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Your employer brand becomes a credential that directly sets your salary floor at your next job; small company vs. large company background produces dramatically different next-offer starting points
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check if the company appears on target-company lists used by top recruiters; assess whether peers with this company on their resume get interviews at your target next employer

decision_factors.factor: Role type and its market value
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Even within the same company, the role determines your market price at next job — a lower-paid algorithm engineer role today yields higher future offers than a higher-paid QA role today
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research external market rates for the specific role title; assess whether the role is core business or peripheral

decision_factors.factor: Direct manager relationship and reporting structure
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Your direct manager determines your day-to-day happiness, performance review outcomes, and internal promotion chances more than any other single factor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask during interviews: who you report to, their reporting chain, whether you have multi-line reporting (multiple bosses exponentially increases complexity)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A role with fast level progression at a smaller company may outperform a prestigious role where people stagnate for 3-4 years at the same level
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask current employees how long it typically takes to get promoted; check LinkedIn tenure patterns for people in that role

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Poor team culture causes psychological damage over time; a misaligned team is invisible during negotiation but becomes the dominant factor in daily experience
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess during interviews whether the team has shared goals, clear ownership, and mutual trust; watch for blame-shifting or vague accountability

decision_factors.factor: Guaranteed cash compensation (base + signing, excluding unvested equity)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Current cash sets the baseline for future salary negotiations; a lower base today compounds into lower baselines at future jobs
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate only the fully vested, guaranteed cash component; exclude unvested options and promised future raises

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Long commutes cause cumulative physical and psychological fatigue that reduces life satisfaction and work performance; surveys show 93%+ of urban workers in China report commute as a significant stressor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate actual daily round-trip time including transit waits; factor this against total discretionary hours per day

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing the higher-salary offer without considering role type
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A higher-paying QA/testing role locks you into a lower-value job category, making future salary jumps harder even if current pay is better than an algorithm or data engineering role
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career candidates who optimize for immediate income over role-based career capital

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a prestigious large company for the brand value
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Some large companies have very low internal mobility — employees sit at the same level for 3-4 years with minimal raises, negating the brand benefit and losing years of compounding salary growth
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career professionals who assume prestige always translates to growth

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting an offer with attractive unvested equity or promised future raises
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: These are non-guaranteed and should not be counted as real compensation; people who factor them in overestimate their actual total comp and make suboptimal comparisons
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Anyone comparing offers that differ significantly in equity or raise promises

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Ignoring commute time to capture a higher salary
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: 2-3 hour daily commutes produce compounding fatigue and life-quality loss that no salary premium fully compensates for; the psychological toll accumulates invisibly
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who rationally weigh salary but underweight daily time costs

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing a well-aligned team culture over immediate compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The benefit is invisible when things are good but becomes the dominant factor when things go wrong — the 'spiritual damage cost' (精神损失费) of a misaligned team is systematically underestimated at decision time
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who treat culture as a soft/optional factor in an otherwise transactional comparison

failure_patterns.pattern: Comparing offers by raw score totals without applying personal importance weights
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Weighted scoring requires self-knowledge about values; raw totals feel more objective and require less introspection
failure_patterns.consequence: Choosing the wrong offer — the case example shows raw scores favoring Offer A (390 vs 370) while weighted scores strongly favor Offer B (104 vs 69)
warning_signs: Saying 'Offer A scored higher overall so I'll pick it'
Treating all factors as equally important without explicitly assigning weights

failure_patterns.pattern: Counting unvested equity and promised raises as real compensation in offer comparisons
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Recruiters present total comp including equity and raise projections, making it feel like guaranteed income; anchoring bias inflates its perceived value
failure_patterns.consequence: Overestimating one offer's value and making a suboptimal choice based on compensation that may never materialize
warning_signs: Including '4-year vesting schedule' totals in your offer comparison spreadsheet
Factoring in 'up to X% annual raise' language in the offer letter

failure_patterns.pattern: Making offer decisions without first clarifying your core priority
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People feel pressure to decide quickly and skip the introspective step; or they assume their priority is obvious (money) without testing whether it's actually consistent with their constraints
failure_patterns.consequence: Applying inconsistent weights across factors, feeling regret after choosing, or choosing based on others' frameworks rather than your own situation
warning_signs: Asking 'which offer is better?' without specifying your own situation or goals
Borrowing someone else's scoring framework verbatim without adjusting weights

failure_patterns.pattern: Underweighting or ignoring the direct manager when evaluating offers
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Manager quality is hard to assess before joining; candidates focus on observable/quantifiable factors like salary and company brand
failure_patterns.consequence: Ending up with a technically good offer at a good company but miserable daily experience due to an incompatible or poor manager
warning_signs: Not asking about reporting structure during interviews
Not researching the direct manager's background or management style

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual core goal from this job — long-term earnings, career capital, family stability, or passion/achievement?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which framework and factor weights are appropriate for this person's comparison — someone optimizing for money uses a different framework than someone optimizing for family stability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: N/A — clarify the specific goal and rebuild the comparison framework around it
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the person cannot articulate a core goal, they should resolve career direction before comparing offers

diagnostic_questions.question: Does either offer include unvested equity or promised future raises, and are you counting those in your comparison?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is inflating one offer's value with non-guaranteed compensation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Recalculate using only guaranteed, immediately vested cash components
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Comparison is on solid footing; proceed to weighted scoring

diagnostic_questions.question: What role type does each offer involve, and what is that role's external market value trajectory?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether a lower-salary offer in a higher-value role (e.g., ML engineer) will outperform a higher-salary offer in a lower-value role (e.g., QA) at the next job change
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the lower-pay role has higher market value, consider accepting short-term pay cut for long-term career capital
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If roles are equivalent, focus on company prestige and team factors

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you observed the promotion velocity of people currently in this role at this company?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company's prestige advantage is real or offset by internal stagnation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If people are staying at the same level for 3-4 years, the prestige benefit may not outweigh the growth opportunity at a smaller but faster-moving company
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Research LinkedIn profiles of current and former employees in that role to assess typical tenure before promotion

diagnostic_questions.question: Who is your direct manager, what is their reporting line, and will you have multi-line reporting?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether daily work experience will be manageable; multi-line reporting (7-8 bosses) exponentially increases complexity and reduces autonomy
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If multi-line reporting exists, assess whether you've successfully navigated that before and whether it matches your working style
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Single reporting line is simpler; assess the specific manager's style and alignment with your work preferences

industry_realities.common_belief: Pick the offer with the highest total compensation number
industry_realities.actual_reality: Total comp numbers are misleading without applying personal importance weights; and a higher-paying offer in a lower-value role can produce lower lifetime earnings than a lower-paying offer in a high-value role
industry_realities.implication: You need a weighted scoring model calibrated to your own priorities, not just a raw comp comparison

industry_realities.common_belief: Big company always beats small company because of brand and stability
industry_realities.actual_reality: Large companies can have very low internal mobility — employees stagnating at the same level for 3-4 years with low salary growth; a smaller company with fast promotion cycles may produce better career and financial outcomes
industry_realities.implication: You must research actual promotion velocity at the specific large company, not just assume prestige = growth

industry_realities.common_belief: Salary is the most important factor when comparing offers
industry_realities.actual_reality: Multiple experienced commenters independently argue that industry trajectory, company prestige, and role type all outrank current salary because they determine your salary ceiling at every future job
industry_realities.implication: Optimizing for current salary at the expense of career capital is a short-term strategy that compounds negatively over time

industry_realities.common_belief: Team culture and manager quality are soft factors that matter less than hard metrics like pay and brand
industry_realities.actual_reality: The direct manager is described as the single most determinative factor for day-to-day happiness and ultimate success; team culture is described as 'air and water' — invisible when good, severely damaging when bad
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should invest significant interview effort into assessing manager compatibility and team dynamics, treating it as a hard factor

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to compare compensation across offers
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Add up all compensation components including unvested equity and promised raises; pick the highest number
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Count only guaranteed, immediately vested cash; exclude options and raise promises; then apply weighted scoring based on personal priorities
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Counting non-guaranteed comp inflates one offer's apparent value; unweighted totals produce systematically wrong decisions

junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Optimize for the long-term salary trajectory — current salary is just a base that gets multiplied by future job changes; role type, company prestige, and career capital matter more than current figures
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A small salary difference at job 1 compounds into a large lifetime earnings difference because it resets the negotiation baseline at every subsequent job

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treat any large company offer as automatically better due to brand, stability, and prestige
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Verify actual internal promotion velocity and salary growth rate; a prestigious company with low internal mobility may be worse than a smaller company with fast career progression
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Prestige without growth traps people in the same role/level for years while peers at scrappier companies advance faster

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Importance of manager in offer evaluation
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Focus on company-level factors (brand, pay, benefits) and treat manager as unknowable until you start
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Proactively investigate the direct manager during interviews — their reporting line, management style, alignment with your working style — treating manager quality as a top-tier decision factor
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The manager determines performance reviews, promotion decisions, and daily quality of life more than any company-level attribute

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Compare offers by intuition or by the two or three most obvious dimensions (pay, commute, company name)
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Use a structured weighted scoring model: enumerate all relevant dimensions, score each offer on each dimension, assign personal importance weights, multiply and sum — then compare
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Intuitive comparison systematically over-weights salient factors (pay, brand) and under-weights invisible ones (manager, role type, culture), producing regrettable choices

community_misconceptions.misconception: Options (期权) are real compensation and should be counted when comparing offers
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Recruiters present options as part of total comp; large projected values feel concrete even if unvested and contingent on liquidity events
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Options are 'big cakes' (大饼) in most cases — they should be excluded from your offer comparison calculation entirely; only count guaranteed, vested cash
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates accept lower base salary in exchange for options that never vest or never become liquid, ending up with less actual compensation

community_misconceptions.misconception: Promised annual raise percentages should be factored into your offer comparison
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Companies present 'annual review with up to X% raise' as a benefit; it feels like a quantifiable future value
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Annual raise promises are non-guaranteed and vary by performance, company financials, and manager discretion; they should not be counted in your offer comparison
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Overvaluing one offer based on raise promises, then receiving minimal or no raises, while the competing offer's actual guaranteed compensation would have been superior

community_misconceptions.misconception: The offer with the highest raw score across all factors is the right choice
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Summing scores feels rigorous and objective; people equate 'higher number' with 'better choice'
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Raw scores without personal importance weights are meaningless; the correct method multiplies each factor's score by its importance weight before summing
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Choosing the wrong offer — the worked example in the source shows raw scores favoring Offer A while weighted scores strongly favor Offer B

real_case_outcomes.situation: Candidate comparing Offer A (higher pay, longer commute, less growth potential) vs Offer B (lower pay, shorter commute, faster promotion opportunity) using raw score totals
real_case_outcomes.decision: Initially appeared to choose Offer A based on raw total (390 vs 370)
real_case_outcomes.outcome: After applying weighted scoring with personal importance weights, Offer B scored 104 vs Offer A's 69 — a large reversal showing Offer B was the correct choice
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Weighted scoring can completely reverse a raw-score decision; never compare offers without applying personal importance weights calibrated to your own priorities

real_case_outcomes.situation: Professional who left a job because internal approval processes were too bureaucratic, requiring multiple rounds of sign-off for even small initiatives
real_case_outcomes.decision: Resigned from the role despite presumably acceptable pay and team
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Left due to loss of autonomy and sense of achievement caused by process friction
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Decision-making autonomy (权利) is a factor that is hard to assess before joining but becomes a primary driver of resignation; candidates should explicitly investigate approval processes and decision-making latitude during interviews

psychological_barriers.trigger: Posting 'I have 3 offers, which is better?' without providing personal context, priorities, or situation
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Decision paralysis combined with externalized locus of control — the person wants someone else to make the decision for them to avoid ownership of the outcome
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Asking strangers to compare offers by name alone, as if there is an objectively correct answer independent of the person's goals
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Redirect: 'I can't answer that without knowing your core goal — what are you actually trying to get from this job in the next 3-5 years?' Force the person to own the priority-setting step before any comparison begins

psychological_barriers.trigger: Framing the offer choice as a binary between a higher-salary and a lower-salary option with no other dimensions mentioned
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Salary anchoring bias — salary is the most visible and easily comparable dimension, so it crowds out all other factors in the mental model
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: The person reduces a multi-dimensional decision to a single number comparison, treating salary as a proxy for total offer quality
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Expand the frame: 'Salary is only one of six dimensions. What role type is each offer? What company prestige? What team? Your salary in 5 years depends far more on those than on the current number.'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Expressing fear of 'choosing wrong and regretting for life' when comparing job offers
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Loss aversion and catastrophizing — treating a reversible career decision as permanent and existentially high-stakes
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Paralysis, over-analysis, seeking external validation, delaying a decision beyond the offer deadline
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Normalize reversibility: 'Every job is a stepping stone. The question isn't which offer is perfect — it's which offer gives you better options for your next move. You can course-correct.'

reframing_moves.original_framing: Which offer pays more / which company is bigger?
reframing_moves.reframe: Which offer gives you better long-term earnings trajectory, not just the highest number today?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the comparison from a static snapshot (current salary) to a dynamic model (career capital, role market value, company as resume credential), which is the actual variable that matters over a career
reframing_moves.example_language: 你的核心诉求是长期，稳定，可增长的钱，而非短期支票 ('Your core need is long-term, stable, growing income — not a short-term check')

reframing_moves.original_framing: I can't decide between these two offers — can you help me choose?
reframing_moves.reframe: Before comparing offers, you need to clarify your core need — without that, no framework will give you the right answer
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Forces the person to take ownership of their own value hierarchy before applying any evaluation tool; prevents borrowing someone else's framework that doesn't match their situation
reframing_moves.example_language: 同一个Offer，对不同的人来说，是完全不同的意义 ('The same offer means completely different things to different people')

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I go to the big company or the small company?
reframing_moves.reframe: Which option increases your career capital (experience value, role market price, resume credential) faster?
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the false binary of 'big = safe/good, small = risky/bad' and replaces it with a growth-rate comparison that accounts for stagnation risk at large companies
reframing_moves.example_language: 逆向思维，你希望你的简历上出现什么经验？你觉得哪个offer带来的经验更有含金量？ ('Reverse-engineer: what experience do you want on your resume? Which offer's experience is worth more?')

reframing_moves.original_framing: The higher-scoring offer in total points is obviously better
reframing_moves.reframe: Raw scores without weights are meaningless — the same offer scored by two different people with different priorities should produce different outcomes
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the false objectivity of raw totals and introduces the necessary step of personal values calibration, which is where the real decision actually lives
reframing_moves.example_language: 打分需要按照你自己的想法来，不需要参考别人的分数 ('The scoring must reflect your own judgment — you don't need to reference anyone else's scores')
